claim: Seasonal influenza viruses create a persistent global disease burden by evolving to escape immunity induced by prior infections and vaccinations.
source: Seasonal influenza viruses create a persistent global disease burden by evolving to escape immunity induced by prior infections and vaccinations.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in influenza virology supported by extensive literature and scientific consensus.

claim: New antigenic variants have a substantial selective advantage at the population level.
source: New antigenic variants have a substantial selective advantage at the population level, but these variants are rarely selected within-host, even in previously immune individuals.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to population-level dynamics and is consistent with established understanding of influenza evolution.

claim: New antigenic variants are rarely selected within-host, even in previously immune individuals.
source: New antigenic variants have a substantial selective advantage at the population level, but these variants are rarely selected within-host, even in previously immune individuals.
evidence: This is a key observation that the paper addresses, supported by empirical NGS studies cited later in the manuscript.

claim: Antibody-mediated immunity exerts evolutionary selection pressure on the antigenic phenotype of seasonal influenza viruses.
source: Antibody-mediated immunity exerts evolutionary selection pressure on the antigenic phenotype of seasonal influenza viruses (Hensley et al., 2009; Archetti and Horsfall, 1950).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Influenza virus infections and vaccinations induce neutralizing antibodies that can prevent reinfection with previously encountered virus antigenic variants.
source: Influenza virus infections and vaccinations induce neutralizing antibodies that can prevent reinfection with previously encountered virus antigenic variants, but such reinfections nonetheless occur (Clements et al., 1986; Memoli et al., 2020; Javaid et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Reinfections with previously encountered virus antigenic variants nonetheless occur despite neutralizing antibodies.
source: Influenza virus infections and vaccinations induce neutralizing antibodies that can prevent reinfection with previously encountered virus antigenic variants, but such reinfections nonetheless occur (Clements et al., 1986; Memoli et al., 2020; Javaid et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to empirical studies showing reinfections.

claim: Accumulation of antibody-mediated immunity creates selection pressure favoring antigenic novelty at the human population level.
source: At the human population level, accumulation of antibody-mediated immunity creates selection pressure favoring antigenic novelty.
evidence: This is inferred from the dynamics of immunity and virus evolution at the population scale.

claim: Circulating antigenic variants typically go extinct rapidly following the population-level emergence of a new antigenic variant, at least for A/H3N2 viruses.
source: Circulating antigenic variants typically go extinct rapidly following the population-level emergence of a new antigenic variant, at least for A/H3N2 viruses (Smith et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Smith et al., 2004.

claim: New antigenic variants like those that result in antigenic cluster transitions are likely to be produced in every infected host.
source: New antigenic variants like those that result in antigenic cluster transitions (Smith et al., 2004) and warrant updating the composition of seasonal influenza virus vaccines are likely to be produced in every infected host.
evidence: This is inferred from the high mutation rate, large population sizes, and single amino acid substitution effects described in the following sentences.

claim: Seasonal influenza viruses have high polymerase error rates on the order of 10−5 mutations/nucleotide/replication.
source: Seasonal influenza viruses have high polymerase error rates (on the order of 10−5 mutations/nucleotide/replication [Nobusawa and Sato, 2006]), reach large within-host virus population sizes (as many as 1010 virions [Perelson et al., 2012]), and can be altered antigenically by single amino acid substitutions in the hemagglutinin (HA) protein (Koel et al., 2013; Linderman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nobusawa and Sato, 2006.

claim: Seasonal influenza viruses reach large within-host virus population sizes as many as 1010 virions.
source: Seasonal influenza viruses have high polymerase error rates (on the order of 10−5 mutations/nucleotide/replication [Nobusawa and Sato, 2006]), reach large within-host virus population sizes (as many as 1010 virions [Perelson et al., 2012]), and can be altered antigenically by single amino acid substitutions in the hemagglutinin (HA) protein (Koel et al., 2013; Linderman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Perelson et al., 2012.

claim: Seasonal influenza viruses can be altered antigenically by single amino acid substitutions in the hemagglutinin (HA) protein.
source: Seasonal influenza viruses have high polymerase error rates (on the order of 10−5 mutations/nucleotide/replication [Nobusawa and Sato, 2006]), reach large within-host virus population sizes (as many as 1010 virions [Perelson et al., 2012]), and can be altered antigenically by single amino acid substitutions in the hemagglutinin (HA) protein (Koel et al., 2013; Linderman et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Koel et al., 2013 and Linderman et al., 2014.

claim: In the absence of antibody-mediated selection pressure, de novo generated antigenic variants should constitute a tiny minority of the total within-host virus population.
source: In the absence of antibody-mediated selection pressure, de novo generated antigenic variants should constitute a tiny minority of the total within-host virus population.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutation rate and population dynamics in the absence of selection.

claim: Minority variants are unlikely to be transmitted onward or detected with current next-generation sequencing (NGS) methods.
source: Such minority variants are unlikely to be transmitted onward or detected with current next-generation sequencing (NGS) methods.
evidence: This is inferred from the low frequency of minority variants and the detection limits of NGS.

claim: Selection pressure imposed by the antibody-mediated immune response in previously exposed individuals could promote antigenic variants to sufficiently high frequencies to make them easily transmissible and NGS detectable.
source: But selection pressure imposed by the antibody-mediated immune response in previously exposed individuals could promote these variants to sufficiently high frequencies to make them easily transmissible and NGS detectable.
evidence: This is a theoretical expectation based on the principles of natural selection.

claim: The potential for antibody-mediated antigenic selection can be readily observed in infections of vaccinated mice.
source: The potential for antibody-mediated antigenic selection can be readily observed in infections of vaccinated mice (Hensley et al., 2009) and in virus passage in eggs in the presence of immune sera (Davis et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hensley et al., 2009.

claim: The potential for antibody-mediated antigenic selection can be readily observed in virus passage in eggs in the presence of immune sera.
source: The potential for antibody-mediated antigenic selection can be readily observed in infections of vaccinated mice (Hensley et al., 2009) and in virus passage in eggs in the presence of immune sera (Davis et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Davis et al., 2018.

claim: New antigenic variants are rarely observed in human seasonal influenza virus infections, even in recently infected or vaccinated hosts.
source: Surprisingly, new antigenic variants are rarely observed in human seasonal influenza virus infections, even in recently infected or vaccinated hosts (Debbink et al., 2017; Dinis et al., 2016; McCrone et al., 2018; Sobel Leonard et al., 2016; Han et al., 2019; Valesano et al., 2019; Javaid et al., 2020; Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to NGS studies and by data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: The rarity of new antigenic variants in human infections contradicts existing models of within-host influenza virus evolution.
source: These observations contradict existing models of within-host influenza virus evolution (Luo et al., 2012; Volkov et al., 2010) and pathogen immune escape generally (Kennedy and Read, 2017), which model strong within-host antibody selection from the beginning of infection and therefore predict that new antigenic variants will be at consensus or fixation in detectable reinfections of previously immune hosts.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior modeling studies.

claim: Existing models predict that new antigenic variants will be at consensus or fixation in detectable reinfections of previously immune hosts.
source: These observations contradict existing models of within-host influenza virus evolution (Luo et al., 2012; Volkov et al., 2010) and pathogen immune escape generally (Kennedy and Read, 2017), which model strong within-host antibody selection from the beginning of infection and therefore predict that new antigenic variants will be at consensus or fixation in detectable reinfections of previously immune hosts.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior modeling studies.

claim: Antibody immunity at the point of transmission in previously-infected or vaccinated individuals should reduce the initial probability of reinfection.
source: Antibody immunity at the point of transmission in previously-infected or vaccinated individuals should reduce the initial probability of reinfection (Le Sage et al., 2020); secretory IgA antibodies on mucosal surfaces (sIgA) are likely to play a large role (Wang et al., 2017, see Appendix Section A2).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Le Sage et al., 2020 and Wang et al., 2017.

claim: Secretory IgA antibodies on mucosal surfaces (sIgA) are likely to play a large role in reducing the initial probability of reinfection.
source: Antibody immunity at the point of transmission in previously-infected or vaccinated individuals should reduce the initial probability of reinfection (Le Sage et al., 2020); secretory IgA antibodies on mucosal surfaces (sIgA) are likely to play a large role (Wang et al., 2017, see Appendix Section A2).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2017.

claim: If viruses successfully infect host cells, an antibody-mediated recall response takes multiple days to mount.
source: But if viruses are not blocked at the point of transmission and successfully infect host cells, an antibody-mediated recall response takes multiple days to mount (Coro et al., 2006; Lam and Baumgarth, 2019, see detailed review in Appendix Section A2).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Coro et al., 2006 and Lam and Baumgarth, 2019.

claim: Virus titer may peak before the production of new antibodies has even begun.
source: Virus titer—and virus shedding (Lau et al., 2010)—may peak before the production of new antibodies has even begun, leaving limited opportunity for within-host immune selection.
evidence: This is inferred from the timing of virus replication and antibody response, with a citation to Lau et al., 2010 for virus shedding.

claim: Virus shedding may peak before the production of new antibodies has even begun.
source: Virus titer—and virus shedding (Lau et al., 2010)—may peak before the production of new antibodies has even begun, leaving limited opportunity for within-host immune selection.
evidence: This is inferred from the timing of virus replication and antibody response, with a citation to Lau et al., 2010.

claim: Prior work has established tight population bottlenecks at the point of influenza virus transmission.
source: Moreover, prior work has established tight population bottlenecks at the point of influenza virus transmission (McCrone et al., 2018; Xue and Bloom, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to McCrone et al., 2018 and Xue and Bloom, 2019.

claim: With a tight transmission bottleneck and weak selection during virus exponential growth, antigenic diversity generated during any particular infection will most likely be lost.
source: With a tight transmission bottleneck and weak selection during virus exponential growth, antigenic diversity generated during any particular infection will most likely be lost, slowing the accumulation of population-level antigenic diversity.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of tight bottlenecks and weak selection.

claim: Antibody neutralization at the point of inoculation can protect experienced hosts against reinfection and explain new antigenic variants' population-level selective advantage.
source: We found three modeling results: (1) antibody neutralization at the point of inoculation can protect experienced hosts against reinfection and explain new antigenic variants' population-level selective advantage.
evidence: This is a modeling result from the study.

claim: If successful reinfection occurs, the delay between the start of virus replication and the mounting of a recall antibody response renders within-host antigenic evolution nearly neutral, even in experienced hosts.
source: (2) If successful reinfection occurs, the delay between the start of virus replication and the mounting of a recall antibody response renders within-host antigenic evolution nearly neutral, even in experienced hosts.
evidence: This is a modeling result from the study.

claim: Substantial population immunity may need to accumulate before new antigenic variants are likely to be observed in large numbers at the population level.
source: (3) It is therefore reasonable that substantial population immunity may need to accumulate before new antigenic variants are likely to observed in large numbers at the population level, whereas effective within-host selection would predict that they should be readily observable even before they proliferate.
evidence: This is a modeling result and inference from the study.

claim: Seasonal influenza virus infections of otherwise healthy individuals typically last 5–7 days.
source: (1) Seasonal influenza virus infections of otherwise healthy individuals typically last 5–7 days (Suess et al., 2012);
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Suess et al., 2012.

claim: In influenza virus-naive individuals, it can take up to 7 days for anti-influenza virus antibodies to start being produced.
source: (2) In influenza virus-naive individuals, it can take up to 7 days for anti-influenza virus antibodies to start being produced (Wrammert et al., 2008), effectively resulting in no selection (Figure 1A);
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wrammert et al., 2008 and Figure 1A.

claim: In previously infected ('experienced') individuals, sIgA antibodies can neutralize inoculated virions before they can infect host cells.
source: (3) In previously infected ('experienced') individuals, sIgA antibodies can neutralize inoculated virions before they can infect host cells; (Wang et al., 2017)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2017.

claim: If an inoculated virion manages to cause an infection in an experienced individual, it takes 2–5 days for the infected host to mount a recall adaptive immune response, including producing new antibodies.
source: (4) However, if an inoculated virion manages to cause an infection in an experienced individual, it takes 2–5 days for the infected host to mount a recall adaptive immune response, including producing new antibodies (Coro et al., 2006; Zuccarino-Catania et al., 2014) (see Appendix Section A2 for further discussion of motivating immunology).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Coro et al., 2006 and Zuccarino-Catania et al., 2014.

claim: Previous within-host models have assumed that antibody-mediated neutralization of virions during virus replication is strong from the point of inoculation onward and is the mechanism of protection against reinfection.
source: Importantly, this contrasts with previous within-host models of virus evolution, which have assumed that antibody-mediated neutralization of virions during virus replication is strong from the point of inoculation onward and is the mechanism of protection against reinfection (Luo et al., 2012; Volkov et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Luo et al., 2012 and Volkov et al., 2010.

claim: There is new animal model evidence of sterilizing antibody immunity.
source: It also reflects new animal model evidence of sterilizing antibody immunity (Le Sage et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Le Sage et al., 2020.

claim: Sufficiently strong antibody neutralization during the virus exponential growth period can potentially stop replication and block onward transmission.
source: In our model, sufficiently strong antibody neutralization during the virus exponential growth period can potentially stop replication and block onward transmission, but this mechanism of protection results in detectable new antigenic variants in each observable homotypic reinfection, since the infection is terminated rapidly unless it generates a new antigenic variant that substantially escapes antibody neutralization (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a modeling result shown in Figure 2.

claim: If antibody neutralization during replication is sufficiently strong to control the infection, this mechanism results in detectable new antigenic variants in each observable homotypic reinfection.
source: In our model, sufficiently strong antibody neutralization during the virus exponential growth period can potentially stop replication and block onward transmission, but this mechanism of protection results in detectable new antigenic variants in each observable homotypic reinfection, since the infection is terminated rapidly unless it generates a new antigenic variant that substantially escapes antibody neutralization (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a modeling result shown in Figure 2.

claim: If there is antibody neutralization throughout virus exponential growth and it is not sufficiently strong to control the infection, this facilitates the establishment of new antigenic variants.
source: If there is antibody neutralization throughout virus exponential growth and it is not sufficiently strong to control the infection, this facilitates the establishment of new antigenic variants: variants can be generated de novo and then selected to detectable and easily transmissible frequencies (Figure 1C,D,F, sensitivity analysis in Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: This is a modeling result shown in Figure 1C,D,F and Appendix 1—figure 3.

claim: Adding a realistic delay to antibody production of two days post-infection curtails antigenic replication selection.
source: Adding a realistic delay to antibody production of two days post-infection (Lam and Baumgarth, 2019) curtails antigenic replication selection.
evidence: This is a modeling result with a citation to Lam and Baumgarth, 2019 for the timing.

claim: With a realistic delay in antibody production, there is no focused antibody-mediated response during the virus exponential growth phase, and so the infection is dominated by old antigenic variant virus.
source: There is no focused antibody-mediated response during the virus exponential growth phase, and so the infection is dominated by old antigenic variant virus (Figure 1C,D,G, sensitivity analysis in Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: This is a modeling result shown in Figure 1C,D,G and Appendix 1—figure 3.

claim: Antigenic variant viruses begin to be selected to higher frequencies late in infection, once a memory response produces high concentrations of cross-reactive antibodies.
source: Antigenic variant viruses begin to be selected to higher frequencies late in infection, once a memory response produces high concentrations of cross-reactive antibodies.
evidence: This is a modeling result.

claim: By the time antibodies are produced late in infection, both new antigenic variant and old antigenic variant populations have peaked and begun to decline due to innate immunity and depletion of infectible cells, so new antigenic variants remain too rare to be detectable with NGS.
source: But by the time this happens in typical infections, both new antigenic variant and old antigenic variant populations have peaked and begun to decline due to innate immunity and depletion of infectible cells, so new antigenic variants remain too rare to be detectable with NGS (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a modeling result shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Replication selection of antigenic novelty to detectable levels becomes likely only if infections are prolonged, and virus antigenic diversity and antibody selection pressure therefore coincide.
source: We find that replication selection of antigenic novelty to detectable levels becomes likely only if infections are prolonged, and virus antigenic diversity and antibody selection pressure therefore coincide (Figure 1G, see also Figure 7).
evidence: This is a modeling result shown in Figure 1G and Figure 7.

claim: Within-host adaptive antigenic evolution can be seen in prolonged infections of immune-compromised hosts.
source: This can explain existing observations: within-host adaptive antigenic evolution can be seen in prolonged infections of immune-compromised hosts (Xue et al., 2017), and prolonged influenza infections show large within-host effective population sizes (Lumby et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Xue et al., 2017 and Lumby et al., 2020.

claim: Prolonged influenza infections show large within-host effective population sizes.
source: This can explain existing observations: within-host adaptive antigenic evolution can be seen in prolonged infections of immune-compromised hosts (Xue et al., 2017), and prolonged influenza infections show large within-host effective population sizes (Lumby et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lumby et al., 2020.

claim: Adding antibody neutralization of virions at the point of inoculation to the model produces realistic levels of protection against reinfection.
source: Adding antibody neutralization of virions at the point of inoculation (e.g. by mucosal sIgA) to our model produces realistic levels of protection against reinfection, and when reinfections do occur, they are overwhelmingly old antigenic variant reinfections.
evidence: This is a modeling result.

claim: When reinfections occur with mucosal antibody neutralization, they are overwhelmingly old antigenic variant reinfections.
source: Adding antibody neutralization of virions at the point of inoculation (e.g. by mucosal sIgA) to our model produces realistic levels of protection against reinfection, and when reinfections do occur, they are overwhelmingly old antigenic variant reinfections.
evidence: This is a modeling result.

claim: New antigenic variants that arise during reinfections with mucosal antibody neutralization remain undetectably rare, reproducing observations from natural human infections.
source: New antigenic variants that arise during these reinfections remain undetectably rare, reproducing observations from natural human infections (Figures 1A–D,G–H, Figure 3B–C; Debbink et al., 2017; Dinis et al., 2016; McCrone et al., 2018; Sobel Leonard et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a modeling result that reproduces empirical observations, supported by citations and figures.

claim: The combination of mucosal sIgA protection and a realistically-timed antibody recall response explains how there can exist immune protection against reinfection without observable within-host antigenic selection in typical infections of experienced hosts.
source: The combination of mucosal sIgA protection and a realistically-timed antibody recall response explains how there can exist immune protection against reinfection—and thus a population-level selective advantage for new antigenic variants—without observable within-host antigenic selection in typical infections of experienced hosts.
evidence: This is a key conclusion from the modeling results.

claim: An antigenic variant that has been generated de novo within a host must survive a series of population bottlenecks if it is to infect other individuals.
source: Regardless of host immune status, an antigenic variant that has been generated de novo within a host must survive a series of population bottlenecks if it is to infect other individuals.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the transmission process.

claim: The sum of all bottleneck effects is the net bottleneck and typically results in infections being initiated by a single genomic variant.
source: The sum of all of these effects is the net bottleneck and typically results in infections being initiated by a single genomic variant (McCrone et al., 2018; Xue and Bloom, 2019; Ghafari et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to McCrone et al., 2018, Xue and Bloom, 2019, and Ghafari et al., 2020.

claim: Bottlenecks resulting from direct contact transmission may be substantially wider than those associated with respiratory droplet or aerosol transmission.
source: That said, bottlenecks resulting from direct contact transmission may be substantially wider than those associated with respiratory droplet or aerosol transmission (Varble et al., 2014) and more human studies are required to quantify these differences.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Varble et al., 2014.

claim: Because antigenic variants appear at very low within-host frequencies when generated de novo and undergo minimal or no replication selection, new antigenic variants most commonly reach detectable levels within hosts through founder effects at the point of inter-host transmission.
source: We find that because antigenic variants appear at very low within-host frequencies when generated de novo and undergo minimal or no replication selection, new antigenic variants most commonly reach detectable levels within hosts through founder effects at the point of inter-host transmission: a low-frequency antigenic variant generated in one host survives the net bottleneck to found the infection of a second host (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a modeling result shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Given that influenza bottlenecks are thought to be on the order of a single virion, any replication-competent mutant that founds an infection should occur at NGS-detectable levels, and likely at consensus.
source: Given that influenza bottlenecks are thought to be on the order of a single virion (McCrone et al., 2018), any replication-competent mutant that founds an infection should occur at NGS-detectable levels, and likely at consensus.
evidence: This is inferred from the tight bottleneck size, with a citation to McCrone et al., 2018.

claim: Founder effects that promote new variants to consensus are rare events.
source: But for the same reason, these founder effects are rare events.
evidence: This is inferred from the low frequency of new variants and the tight bottleneck.

claim: The sampling process that produces founder effects could be purely neutral in a truly naive recipient host who does not possess well-matched antibodies to the inoculated old variant.
source: The sampling process that produces these founder effects could be a purely neutral. It is likely quite close to neutral in a truly naive recipient host who does not possess well-matched antibodies to the inoculated old variant: all inoculated virions, regardless of antigenic phenotype, have an equal chance of becoming part of the new infection's founding population.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of selection in naive hosts.

claim: New antigenic variant infections of naive hosts should occur on the order of 1 in 105 or 1 in 104 such infections given biologically plausible parameters.
source: New antigenic variant infections of naive hosts should then occur on the order of 1 in 105 or 1 in 104 such infections given biologically plausible parameters (Figure 3E–H).
evidence: This is a modeling result shown in Figure 3E–H.

claim: If different virions have different chances of being neutralized at the point of transmission, the founding process may be selective.
source: But if different virions have different chances of being neutralized at the point of transmission, the founding process may be selective.
evidence: This is inferred from differential neutralization probabilities.

claim: Among virions that encounter antibodies, those that are less likely to be neutralized have a higher than average chance of undergoing stochastic promotion to consensus.
source: Among the virions that encounter antibodies, those that are less likely to be neutralized have a higher than average chance of undergoing stochastic promotion to consensus while those that are more likely to be neutralized have a lower than average chance.
evidence: This is inferred from differential neutralization probabilities.

claim: A new antigenic variant may be disproportionately likely to survive the net bottleneck due to differential neutralization.
source: A new antigenic variant may then be disproportionately likely to survive the net bottleneck (Figure 3, Appendix Section A4.2).
evidence: This is a modeling result shown in Figure 3.

claim: Neutralization at the point of transmission not only gives new antigenic variant infections their transmission advantage but may also increase the rate at which these new antigenic variant infections arise.
source: Neutralization at the point of transmission thus not only gives new antigenic variant infections their transmission advantage (population-level selection) but may also increase the rate at which these new antigenic variant infections arise (inoculation selection).
evidence: This is a modeling result and inference.

claim: There is some suggestive evidence of differential survival of particular influenza genetic variants at the point of transmission from experiments in ferrets.
source: There is some suggestive evidence of differential survival of particular (not necessarily antigenic) influenza genetic variants at the point of transmission from experiments in ferrets (Wilker et al., 2013; Moncla et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wilker et al., 2013 and Moncla et al., 2016.

claim: It is difficult empirically to distinguish selection that occurs at the point of transmission from selection that occurs during early replication in the recipient host because of the challenges associated with sampling the small virus populations present at the earliest stages of infection.
source: But as Lumby and colleagues (Lumby et al., 2018) point out in a reanalysis of those experiments, it is difficult empirically to distinguish selection that occurs at the point of transmission from selection that occurs during early replication in the recipient host because of the challenges associated with sampling the small virus populations present at the earliest stages of infection.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lumby et al., 2018.

claim: The strength of inoculation selection depends on the ratio of the number of virions that compete to found an infection in the absence of well-matched sIgA antibodies to the number of virions that actually found an infection.
source: The strength of inoculation selection depends on the ratio of the number of virions that compete to found an infection in the absence of well-matched sIgA antibodies (the mucus bottleneck size v) to the number of virions that actually found an infection (the final cell infection bottleneck size b).
evidence: This is a modeling result.

claim: When new antigenic variant immune escape is incomplete due to partial cross-reactivity with previous antigenic variants, increased antibody neutralization is a double-edged sword for new antigenic variant virions.
source: When new antigenic variant immune escape is incomplete due to partial cross-reactivity with previous antigenic variants, increased antibody neutralization is a double-edged sword for new antigenic variant virions. Competition to found the infection from old antigenic variant virions is reduced, but the new antigenic variant is itself at greater risk of being neutralized.
evidence: This is a modeling result and inference.

claim: An experienced recipient host could facilitate the survival of large-effect antigenic variants while impeding the survival of variants that provide less substantial immune escape.
source: An experienced recipient host could facilitate the survival of large-effect antigenic variants (like those seen at antigenic cluster transitions [Smith et al., 2004]) while impeding the survival of variants that provide less substantial immune escape (Figure 3E, Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: This is a modeling result shown in Figure 3E and Appendix 1—figure 1, with a citation to Smith et al., 2004.

claim: At realistic parameter values and assuming all individuals develop well-matched antibodies to previously encountered antigenic variants, only ∼1 to 2 in 104 inoculations of an experienced host results in a new antigenic variant surviving the bottleneck.
source: At realistic parameter values and assuming all individuals develop well-matched antibodies to previously encountered antigenic variants, only ∼1 to 2 in 104 inoculations of an experienced host results in a new antigenic variant surviving the bottleneck (Figure 4E,H, Figure 4).
evidence: This is a modeling result shown in Figure 4.

claim: The rate of new variant bottleneck survival in experienced hosts is likely to be an overestimate due to various factors.
source: This rate is likely to be an overestimate due to the factors mentioned above.
evidence: This is inferred from the limitations discussed.

claim: The rate of new variant bottleneck survival in experienced hosts is only about 2- to 3-fold higher than the rate of bottleneck survival in naive hosts.
source: Moreover, it is only about 2- to 3-fold higher than the rate of bottleneck survival in naive hosts, where new antigenic variant infections should occasionally occur via neutral stochastic founder effects.
evidence: This is a modeling result comparing experienced and naive hosts.

claim: Even in the presence of experienced hosts, antigenic selection is inefficient and most generated antigenic diversity is lost at the point of transmission.
source: In short, even in the presence of experienced hosts, antigenic selection is inefficient and most generated antigenic diversity is lost at the point of transmission.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling results.

claim: Because of the inefficiencies of antigenic selection, new antigenic variants can be generated in every infected host without producing explosive antigenic diversification at the population level.
source: Because of these inefficiencies, new antigenic variants can be generated in every infected host without producing explosive antigenic diversification at the population level.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the modeling results.

claim: When all hosts in a model transmission chain are naive, antigenic evolution is non-directional and recapitulates the distribution of within-host mutations.
source: When all hosts in a model transmission chain are naive, antigenic evolution is non-directional and recapitulates the distribution of within-host mutations (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is a modeling result shown in Figure 5A.

claim: When antigenic selection is constant throughout infection and even a moderate fraction of hosts are experienced, antigenic evolution is unrealistically adaptive: the virus evolves directly away from existing immunity and large-effect antigenic changes are observed frequently.
source: When antigenic selection is constant throughout infection and even a moderate fraction of hosts are experienced, antigenic evolution is unrealistically adaptive: the virus evolves directly away from existing immunity and large-effect antigenic changes are observed frequently (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is a modeling result shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: When the model incorporates both mucosal antibodies and realistically-timed recall responses, major antigenic variants appear only rarely and the overall distribution of emerged variants better mimics empirical observations.
source: When the model incorporates both mucosal antibodies and realistically-timed recall responses, major antigenic variants appear only rarely and the overall distribution of emerged variants better mimics empirical observations (Figure 5D)—most notably, the phenomenon of quasi-neutral diversification within an antigenic cluster seen in Figures 1 and 2 of Smith et al., 2004.
evidence: This is a modeling result shown in Figure 5D, with a citation to Smith et al., 2004.

claim: An immediate recall response would predict strong near-constant directed evolution of virus antigenic phenotypes away from existing immunity.
source: In particular, we note that whereas an immediate recall response would predict strong near-constant directed evolution of virus antigenic phenotypes away from existing immunity (Figure 5B,C), a realistically-timed recall response predicts that small-effect, drift-like antigenic substitutions will be observed.
evidence: This is a modeling result shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: A realistically-timed recall response predicts that small-effect, drift-like antigenic substitutions will be observed.
source: In particular, we note that whereas an immediate recall response would predict strong near-constant directed evolution of virus antigenic phenotypes away from existing immunity (Figure 5B,C), a realistically-timed recall response predicts that small-effect, drift-like antigenic substitutions will be observed.
evidence: This is a modeling result.

claim: Even substitutions that move a virus 'backward' in antigenic space can be observed thanks to the large role of stochasticity at the point of transmission.
source: Even substitutions that move a virus 'backward' in antigenic space—﻿so that it is more readily neutralized by existing antibodies than the ancestral variant—can be observed thanks to the large role of stochasticity at the point of transmission.
evidence: This is a modeling result.

claim: There is a slight bias favoring forward substitutions, especially those of sufficiently large effect to create a substantial selective advantage over the ancestral variant.
source: That said, there is a slight bias favoring forward substitutions, especially those of sufficiently large effect to create a substantial selective advantage over the ancestral variant (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a modeling result shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The model predicts the observed pattern of quasi-neutral diversification within antigenic clusters followed by rarer directional 'jumps' in phenotype.
